title: New Public Charge Rule Takes Effect September 18: What Indian Green Card Applicants Must Know
excerpt: DHS rescinds the Biden-era standard and gives officers broader discretion to weigh benefits use, with a hard form-change deadline that leaves no room for error.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has rescinded the 2022 Biden-era public charge regulation, restoring broader officer discretion to weigh applicants' use of means-tested public benefits when deciding green card cases.
  • The new rule takes effect September 18, 2026. USCIS will introduce a revised Form I-485 on the same date, with no grace period — applications filed with the wrong edition will be rejected.
  • Officers will apply a "totality of the circumstances" analysis, potentially considering benefits such as Medicaid, SNAP, housing assistance and CHIP, though using benefits does not trigger automatic denial.
  • For Indian professionals on employment-based tracks, the practical impact may be limited since most maintain stable employment, but the hard form deadline creates a procedural risk for families mid-filing.

What the Rule Changes

The Trump administration finalized a rule on July 20, 2026, rescinding the Biden-era public charge regulation that had narrowed the grounds for denying a green card based on benefits use. The change, announced by DHS and published in the Federal Register, takes effect on September 18, according to Reuters.

Under the 2022 framework being scrapped, only applicants "primarily dependent" on cash assistance or long-term institutional care could be flagged as potential public charges. The new rule removes that bright-line test and hands immigration officers broad discretion to consider a wider range of means-tested public benefits under a "totality of the circumstances" standard.

"Aliens in the United States [should] be self-reliant and not dependent on taxpayer-funded government benefits."

— U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, post on X

DHS has said it will issue additional subregulatory guidance before September 18, but the rule itself does not specify exactly which safety-net programs trigger scrutiny. According to CNN, that could potentially include childcare subsidies, Head Start, the Children's Health Insurance Program and certain tax breaks such as the child tax credit.

The September 18 Deadline

Alongside the substantive policy shift, USCIS will replace the current Form I-485 — the application used to adjust immigration status to permanent residence — with a revised edition dated September 18, 2026. The transition is hard: the current edition must be postmarked or electronically submitted before September 18, while the new edition will only be accepted from that date onward.

There is no overlap period. An applicant who submits the outgoing form on or after September 18 will have their application rejected. One who submits the new form before September 18 faces the same result.

USCIS has released a preview of the revised form to give applicants and attorneys time to prepare, but has made clear it cannot be filed early.

Why This Matters for Indian Applicants

Indian nationals are one of the largest groups of employment-based immigrants in the United States and face some of the longest waits in the green card system. For many highly skilled professionals in technology, healthcare, engineering and finance, filing Form I-485 comes after years of employer-sponsored petitions and priority date waits.

When the filing window finally opens, it can be time-sensitive. A rejected application because of a wrong form edition could force families to reassemble extensive filing packages involving employment records, birth and marriage certificates, medical examinations and financial documentation, according to the South Asian Herald.

The risk is compounded for Indian families because employment-based green card applications frequently involve spouses and children. A form revision affecting the principal applicant can disrupt an entire household's coordinated filing.

Practical Impact on Benefit Use

For most Indian professionals on EB-2 and EB-3 tracks, the practical impact on benefit eligibility may be limited. Most maintain stable employment and already meet financial self-sufficiency requirements. However, DHS estimates that about 950,000 people across all nationalities may choose to leave or not enroll in six public benefits programs it examined, including Medicaid, SNAP, CHIP and federal rental assistance, according to CNN.

Immigration advocates have warned that the rule could create a "chilling effect" in which families disenroll even citizen children from programs they are entitled to, fearing consequences for a pending green card case. DHS acknowledged in the rule that applicants may choose not to enroll citizen children to "avoid negative consequences."

What Applicants Should Do Now

Immigration attorneys recommend several steps before September 18: applicants whose cases are ready should consider whether filing under the current standard is advantageous. Those planning to file after September 18 should review the preview form and prepare accordingly. All applicants should download the form directly from USCIS rather than relying on older copies, and verify the edition date before submission.

Benefits received before September 18 will be assessed under the prior 2022 standard. Benefits applied for on or after the effective date may be considered under the expanded framework. DHS has said it will issue further guidance, and immigration law firms expect additional advisories in the weeks ahead.
nri_angle: Indian nationals, who face some of the longest employment-based green card waits, must navigate a hard September 18 form deadline and new benefits scrutiny under the revised public charge framework.
